title.narrative: SAA Emergency Obstetric Care (EMONC) Diploma Training: Activity # 24860

description.narrative: (1) Direct: health workforce working in public health facilities nationwide, and (2) Indirect: married women at reproductive age (MWRA) and their newborn babies nationwide.

(1) to improve skilled care human resources on EmONC services, particularly comprehensive EmONC, and (2) to increase the availability of competent, responsive, motivated and productive health personnel to ensure women with direct obstetric complications are treated in EmONC facilities.

The Emergency Obstetric Neonatal Care (EmONC) Diploma Training Program funded by the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands (EKN) seeks to assist the government of Yemen in meeting the National Strategy for Reproductive Health and the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) 4 and 5. The program has been initiated in response to the gaps in EmONC staff identified at nationwide level through a rapid needs assessment study conducted with support from EKN and published in October 2012. This study of human Emergency Obstetric & Neonatal Care (EmONC) resources gaps and needs used particularly Emergency Response Team (ERT) approach, which incorporates five personnel categories; obstetricians, neonatologists and anesthesiologists for general practitioners, neonatal nurses and operation theater nurses, to provide EmONC services in comprehensive EmONC hospitals nationwide in Yemen. The study found critical shortages across maternal and newborn health cadres; geographical mal-distribution of the workforce with a heavy bias in urban governorates while other governorates, where with substantial rural areas, are with severe shortage especially of EmONC specialists; imbalances in gender; a growing private sector which reportedly impacts upon attrition and the poor retention of the public sector workforce (especially for physicians). As a result, there is limited access to EmONC services. The lack of and inequity in access to emergency obstetric care and management of problems of the newborns hamper the efforts to reduce maternal and neonatal mortality as targeted in the Millennium Development Goals 4 and 5. The study estimated that 156 obstetricians, 172 neonatologists, 108 anesthesiologists, 81 operating theater nurses, and 775 neonatal nurses are still needed to provide 24-hour comprehensive EmONC services in the 91 EmONC hospitals scheduled to become operational by 2015.
